792.title: Satta and Balvand
792.hook: two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven; their Var is in the Granth (Ramkali, ang 966–968)
792.howItsDone: The Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs tell their story as one of pride, return and forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhatts, poets of praise, who sang the Gurus as one light. Today, two musicians who walked out.

Two musicians, a rebab and a voice, singing kirtan in the Guru's court: Satta and Balvand. Then, tradition says, something goes wrong. A request for money, a quarrel, wounded pride. They stop singing, say hard things about the house they served, and walk out. A falling-out could end right there. This one ends with their song inside the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Ramkali, Ang 966, kept and sung beside the Gurus' own words.
screen: `TWO MUSICIANS IN THE GURU'S COURT.` → `A QUARREL, AND A WALKOUT.` → `THEIR SONG IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First the story, as tradition tells it. Satta and Balvand ask Guru Arjan for help, and when it isn't what they hoped, pride takes over. They refuse to play, and boast that the Gurus' fame rests on their music. Without the court, their fortunes sink. In the end they come back humbled, asking forgiveness, and tradition says a devoted Sikh pleaded for them. The Guru forgives them, and they pick up the rebab again. Now the text, which is what the Granth actually keeps: their Var, a ballad, in Raag Ramkali. It doesn't sing about themselves. It sings about Guru Nanak setting up Lehna as the next Guru, Guru Angad, and the line passing on. One of its lines, in paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the master has only changed the body. It's the claim the Bhatts made yesterday, but listen to who's making it now. Two men who once claimed the Gurus needed them end up singing that the Guru is one light, needing nothing from anyone, passing from body to body. The quarrel was about who mattered. The song answers it: the light matters, and everyone else is a singer. And notice what the Guru did. He didn't just let them back in the door. Their words went into the scripture, sung in gurdwaras alongside his own. Forgiveness here isn't a grudging truce. It's a microphone handed back.

segments.voice: Choose a small quarrel, sized for two minutes: a sharp exchange, a slight, a door that closed, and let the other person's face come to mind. You don't have to call them or pretend it didn't happen; just loosen your grip on it, one breath at a time, and if something in you is ready, imagine handing them their voice back. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.
Var. A ballad: Satta and Balvand's, in Raag Ramkali, singing that the light is the same, the way is the same, only the body has changed.
Your line: forgiven, and sung. The walkout wasn't the end of their story. See you tomorrow.

793.title: The saloks to Mardana
793.hook: a few saloks are headed with Mardana's name, generally read as Nanak's words to him (Bihagra ki Var, ang 553)
793.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana as Guru Nanak's companion and rebab player, and the saloks headed with his name in Bihagra ki Var are read and sung as part of that Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Var: a quarrel, a return, and a song kept in the Granth. Today, the friend who was there first.

Mardana. In the Sikh stories he is close by: Guru Nanak's companion on the road, a Muslim musician with a rebab, playing while Nanak sang. Yesterday's minstrels came later. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Bihagra ki Var, Ang 553. Among the saloks there, a few carry Mardana's name in the heading. They're generally read as Nanak's words to him, friend to friend. And they aren't gentle words.
screen: `MARDANA AND HIS REBAB.` → `HIS NAME IN THE HEADING.` → `NANAK'S WORDS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The saloks begin with a picture a friend might use to tease you awake. In paraphrase: this dark age is the wine jar, desire is the wine, and the mind is the one drinking it. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and ego is the one pouring. Drink in that company, and you're ruined. Strong words. But Nanak doesn't just take the cup away. He offers a different brew. In paraphrase again: make good deeds the vat, truth the sweetener, and truth itself the finest wine. Make goodness the bread and good conduct the butter. That's the drink, he says, that wipes away wrongdoing. So the saloks don't scold the thirst. They redirect it: whatever pulls at you, desire, the need to be filled, take that same longing and point it at truth. Now the heading. Readers differ on what the name Mardana is doing there: whether the words are spoken to him, or carry his name for another reason. The tradition generally hears them as words to a friend, and that changes how they sound. These aren't lines shouted at a crowd. They're what you say to someone you've walked with for years, who can take hard words because they know you love them. Friends name the cup in your hand. Then they hand you a better one.

794.title: Sundar's call
794.hook: Sundar records Guru Amar Das's last wishes: sing the Lord's praise, don't weep for me (Ramkali, Sadd, ang 923)
794.howItsDone: At Sikh funerals kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are central, and the Sadd is sometimes sung; Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul answering God's call home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mardana: hard words between friends, and truth as the better wine. Today, a Guru's last wishes.

Some families keep a letter in a drawer, written to be opened after a parent dies. Sometimes it holds money matters. Sometimes it says: don't make a fuss, play my favorite song, eat well. In Raag Ramkali, on Ang 923, the Guru Granth Sahib keeps something like that letter. A poet named Sundar records what Guru Amar Das asked of his family as his life came to its end. It's called the Sadd, the call.
screen: `A LETTER IN A DRAWER.` → `PLAY MY SONG, DON'T FUSS.` → `THE SADD, ANG 923.`

segments.voice: In the hymn, the call is the one that comes from God at the end of a life, the summons home. Sundar, whom tradition counts in Guru Amar Das's own family, tells it as an eyewitness would. The Guru gathers his family and speaks plainly. In paraphrase: let no one weep for me after I'm gone; the one who weeps does not please me. Then what he wants instead: after me, sing pure kirtan. Send for the Lord's learned ones, and let them read the Lord's story. Let the Lord's Name be heard. Then the line passes on: the Sadd tells how Guru Amar Das names Ram Das as the Guru after him, and the family bows before him. One short hymn, three things side by side: a death, a song, and the light passing on. Look closely at what he asks. He isn't saying grief is wrong for everyone, always. He's saying what he wants for his own going. He sees his death as being called home, so the fitting answer is praise, not wailing. And it's recorded by someone close to him, who could have written only his own sorrow, and instead wrote down the instructions. Tradition carries this into Sikh funerals, where kirtan and the reading of Gurbani are given the center, and the evening prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is recited. Grief comes. The Sadd gives it a song to walk alongside.

If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

Your line: sing, don't weep. It was the Guru's wish for his own going. That's day seven hundred ninety-four.

795.title: Nothing edited out
795.hook: the Gurus kept these voices and sometimes answered them in hymns of their own
795.howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib the Bhagats' compositions appear under their own names, and Sikh teachers point out the places where a Guru's salok stands beside a Bhagat's and takes up its theme.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sadd: Guru Amar Das asked his family not to weep, but to sing. Today, a conversation kept on the page.

A shared document, the kind a team writes together. One person types a paragraph. Someone else disagrees. They could delete it and write their own, or leave a comment in the margin: here's how I'd put it. The paragraph stays, the comment sits beside it, and anyone who opens the file later sees both. The Guru Granth Sahib does something like that with the Bhagats, and it keeps both names on the page.
screen: `A SHARED DOCUMENT.` → `DELETE IT, OR COMMENT BESIDE IT?` → `BOTH STAY ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: For weeks this path has walked through the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid, Ramanand, Jaidev and more. Their words sit in the Granth under their own names. And sometimes, right beside a Bhagat's verse, stands a verse marked with a Guru's name. It happens among Kabir's saloks, and among Farid's, and readers hear some of these as replies. Take one pair, on Ang 1380. Farid says, in paraphrase: cut open my body and not a drop of blood comes out; those steeped in the Lord have no blood left. Right after it, a verse marked with Guru Amar Das's number answers: this body is all blood, and without blood there is no body; what drains from one steeped in the Lord is the blood of greed. Same image, carried a step further. The compilers had an easy move: cut a line a Guru would put differently, or smooth it into the Gurus' own voice. The Granth doesn't. The Bhagat's words keep the Bhagat's name and way of saying it, and the Guru's verse comes in beside it, with the Guru's name. A reader gets the conversation, not just the conclusion. So the Granth isn't one voice talking to itself. It's a house with many speakers, where the Gurus' voice leads and others are honored at the table, by name. And it offers a pattern for ordinary life. When someone says a thing you'd say differently, there are two easy roads: pretend they never said it, or shout it down. The Granth shows a third: keep their words whole, then answer beside them, in your own voice.

796.title: Weaver, shoemaker, barber, king
796.hook: the Bhagats' trades read like a street; that's the point
796.howItsDone: Sikhs point to the Bhagats' different trades and castes as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's teaching that birth sets no limit on devotion, and the langar, where all sit together, puts the same teaching into practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed: Farid's words kept whole, and Guru Amar Das answering beside them. Today, a walk down the Bhagats' street.

A clatter from a loom in a doorway. Next door, someone bent over a shoe, stitching leather. Further on, a barber with a razor and a customer half-shaved. A farmer coming in from the fields with mud on his feet. And at the end of the road, a palace. Walk the names of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib and that's the street you're walking down: weaver, shoemaker, barber, king.
screen: `A LOOM IN A DOORWAY.` → `LEATHER, A RAZOR, A MUDDY FARMER.` → `A PALACE AT THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Some of these trades come from the Bhagats' own mouths. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his hymns, and works the loom into his songs. Namdev says he was born in the house of a calico printer. Ravidas says his family carried the dead cattle, work the caste order of his day looked down on. Others come from tradition: Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne. Side by side, they don't read like a list of holy men from one class. They read like a street. That's the point. Ravidas's own hymns show a town that ranked people by birth, where a leather-worker's touch was counted as polluting. The Granth answers by putting the weaver's song, the leather-worker's song and the king's song on the same pages, in the same raags, under the same honor. The barber's hymn is sung with the same reverence as the king's. Guru Nanak says it in his own words in Raag Asa, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. So the mix of trades isn't decoration. It's the teaching, made visible. You can't hold the Guru Granth Sahib in your hands and keep the street out of it. And it runs both ways: the king isn't shut out either. Pipa's place there is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.

797.title: Bhagats in kirtan
797.hook: their hymns are sung like any other Gurbani
797.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing the Bhagats' shabads in kirtan alongside the Gurus' hymns, in the raag the Granth assigns them, and the congregation listens and bows in the same way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, weaver, shoemaker, barber, king: the Bhagats' trades read like a street, and your line was the whole street. Today, that street starts to sing.

The harmonium is already breathing when the door opens. Three ragis sit on the low platform, one at the tabla. The room is half full: a grandmother with a bag of fruit, two teenagers near the back, a man straight from a night shift. One shabad ends, the tabla settles, and a new one begins. Same raag, same melody family, same heads bowed. Nobody stops to ask who wrote it. But glance at the heading, and the name isn't a Guru's. It's Kabir's.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM IS ALREADY PLAYING.` → `A NEW SHABAD BEGINS.` → `THE HEADING SAYS KABIR.`

segments.voice: The Granth is arranged by raag, the musical mode a hymn is meant to be sung in: Asa, Gauri, Sorath, Dhanasri. When the Gurus' hymns in a raag are done, the Bhagats' hymns follow in that same raag. Kabir in Gauri. Ravidas in Gauri too. Farid in Asa, as we saw a few weeks back. No appendix at the back: they live in the same rooms as the Gurus' words, set to the same music. Each Bhagat hymn has a heading with its raag and the Bhagat's name, often with ji added, a word of respect. That small mark tells the singer what to sing and the listener whose voice is speaking. It doesn't tell anyone to sing it differently. So a ragi can move from a hymn of Guru Arjan straight into one of Namdev, and the tabla doesn't change its manners. The Rahao line, the pause line at the hymn's center, is sung as the refrain, the same way. When the shabad ends, people bow the same way. Sikhs call the hymns of the Granth bani, or gurbani, the Guru's word. The Bhagats' hymns are also called bhagat bani, which names whose voice it is, but they're read and sung as part of the Guru, not as quotations borrowed from outside. A Sikh singing Kabir isn't stepping out of the Guru's house. The whole book is the house. That's why the Bhagats are hard to spot in a gurdwara: their place is marked by a name, not a separate stage.

798.title: One Bhagat a day
798.hook: a week of reading a different Bhagat each morning
798.howItsDone: Some Sikhs read from the Granth each day, and some keep a sehaj path, a slow reading of the whole Granth over time; a reader may also return to favorite shabads by their ang number.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: same raag, same refrain, same bow, and your line, all gurbani. Today, a week ends and a plan begins.

Seven sticky notes on the bathroom mirror. Each has a name and a page number in marker: Ramanand. Bhikhan. Jaidev. Farid. A week of mornings, one voice per morning, before the phone gets a turn. Today does two jobs: it looks back at this week's voices, and it hands over a small plan for the next seven. One Bhagat a day.
screen: `SEVEN NOTES ON A MIRROR.` → `ONE NAME EACH MORNING.` → `A WEEK BACK, A WEEK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the week behind us. Satta and Balvand, the minstrels whose Var, tradition says, was sung after a quarrel was forgiven. The saloks headed with Mardana's name, words to a friend. Sundar's Sadd: Guru Amar Das asking for singing, not weeping. The Gurus answering voices they would put differently, rather than erasing them. The Bhagats' trades, reading like a whole street. And yesterday, all of it sung as gurbani. Now the week ahead. The Granth is long, and a reader can stand at the front of it and not know where to begin, so here's a doorway the size of a morning. The ang, the page number, is the address. Day one, Ramanand in Raag Basant, Ang 1195: a home colored with love. Day two, Bhikhan in Sorath, Ang 659: the Name as medicine. Day three, Jaidev in Gujri, Ang 526, the old poet. Day four, Farid in Asa, Ang 488: the heart and the lips. Day five, Parmanand and Surdas, side by side on Ang 1253. Day six, Ravidas in Gauri, Ang 345, and the city without sorrow he calls Begampura. Day seven, a handful of Kabir's saloks, near the end of the book. Each reading is short; some are a few lines. Read it slowly, once, in Gurmukhi if you can, in a translation if you can't. Then stop. The point isn't covering ground. It's sitting with one voice long enough to hear how it speaks: Farid's longing, Kabir's sharp edge, Ravidas's dream of a city. By the end of the week, the names stop being a list and become people.
screen: `A WEEK OF VOICES, LOOKED BACK ON.` · `THE ANG IS THE ADDRESS.` · `SEVEN MORNINGS, SEVEN BHAGATS.` · `READ ONE SLOWLY, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `ONE A DAY.`

segments.voice: If you can, open to one of those angs now, read a few lines slowly, and close it before the sit. If not, hold Ramanand's line in your own words, why go out looking, when home is colored with love, and breathe with it; if you pray, Waheguru can ride each breath out. When the to-do list pulls at you, let the line call you back.
Ang. A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, the address for a week of mornings, one Bhagat read slowly on each one.
Your line: one a day. One page, one voice, one morning. Day seven hundred ninety-eight, done.
